newsitem.title: USA: O'Leary to seek ways to ease heating oil fears.
newsitem.headline: O'Leary to seek ways to ease heating oil fears.

text.p: Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary pledged Tuesday to look for ways to bolster stockpiles of heating oil to try to ease concern that Americans in the Northeast and Midwest would face high heating bills this winter.
"We want to see how we can mitigate against price increases," O'Leary said. But she said she would not intervene directly to regulate the oil markets.

"This secretary is not proposing that she gets into the regulatory business," she told reporters after meeting with Sens. Joseph Lieberman and Christopher Dodd of Connecticut and Representative Joe Kennedy of Massachusetts, who raised alarm two weeks ago that refiners' heating oil stocks heading into winter were 15 percent below average for this time of year.
About 12 percent of the nation's homes burn oil for heat, and three quarters of supplies are consumed in the Northeast.
In its weekly oil inventory report late Tuesday, the American Petroleum Institute said for the week ended Sept. 27 heating oil stocks were 17.9 million barrels below a year ago.
Total stocks of distillates, which include heating oil and diesel fuel, are already at historical lows and fell 17,000 barrels during the week ended Sept. 27, the API said.

"Through next week, what I've committed to is going back and taking a hard look at some very creative ideas, which will likely require some additional authority," O'Leary said, referring to proposals by the lawmakers for the Energy Department to sell crude oil from the nation's strategic reserve to help build heating oil inventories.
Lawmakers sent a letter to O'Leary two weeks ago stating their concerns about a possible sharp rise in heating oil and diesel fuel prices this winter.
Oil industry groups have said, however, that selling crude oil from the nation's emergency stockpile to raise money to buy heating oil would be counterproductive.

"If you had the government purchase that distillate (including heating oil) for the purpose of building stocks, ... you would clearly raise the price of distillate," said Charles DiBona, president of the American Petroleum Institute, which represents big oil companies.

He said refiners, who now have little incentive to pay the costs of storing heating oil because prices for heating oil futures contracts are below current market prices, would store even less if they thought the government was going to put heating oil onto the market two or three months from now.
But O'Leary said her department would work with other countries that export petroleum products to the United States.
A senior Energy Department official going to Venezuela Tuesday on an unrelated matter "will raise the issue of are there extra barrels to come from Venezuela to the United States," she said.

Northeastern governors concerned about high heating bills for poor people should apply to the Health and Human Services Department for low-income home energy assistance funds, O'Leary said, noting the programme had $400 million available immediately.
